edge_914.relationship: Provincializing Europe: Europe as the silent referent of historical knowledge, the historicism of 'first in Europe, then elsewhere', and European categories held to be both indispensable and inadequate (1992–2000)
edge_914.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History', Representations 37 (1992), pp. 1–26, read in full (the hosted copy's text layer runs words together; spacing restored in quotations): 'insofar as the academic discourse of history—that is, “history” as a discourse produced at the institutional site of the university—is concerned, “Europe” remains the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan,” and so on'; '“Indian” history itself is in a position of subalternity'; 'Europe' and 'India' are 'treated here as hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (p. 1). 'That Europe works as a silent referent in historical knowledge itself becomes obvious in a highly ordinary way': 'Third-world historians feel a need to refer to works in European history; historians of Europe do not feel any need to reciprocate' (p. 2). The everyday paradox is that 'we find these theories, in spite of their inherent ignorance of “us,” eminently useful in understanding our societies' (p. 3). 'Let us call this the project of provincializing “Europe”' (p. 20); it 'does not call for a simplistic, out-of-hand rejection of modernity, liberal values, universals, science, reason, grand narratives, totalizing explanations' (p. 20), and 'must realize within itself its own impossibility' (p. 22). Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction pp. 3–23 read in the publisher's excerpt: historicism 'made modernity or capitalism look ... as something that became global over time, by originating in one place (Europe) and then spreading outside it. This “first in Europe, then elsewhere” structure of global historical time was historicist' (p. 7); it 'came to non-European peoples in the nineteenth century as somebody's way of saying “not yet” to somebody else', and Mill's argument 'consigned Indians, Africans, and other “rude” nations to an imaginary waiting room of history' (p. 8). European thought 'is both indispensable and inadequate', and 'this simultaneous indispensability and inadequacy of social science thought is the task this book has set itself' (p. 6); 'provincializing Europe is not a project of rejecting or discarding European thought' (p. 16). The problem of capitalist modernity is 'a problem of translation, as well' as of transition (p. 17). Chapter 1 'reproduces, in an abridged form, a programmatic statement ... that I published in 1992 in the journal Representations' (p. 19). In-period reception and criticism: Arif Dirlik (Critical Inquiry 20, 1994; read) cites the 1992 essay (p. 334, n. 7) for postcolonial criticism's repudiation of the modes-of-production narrative, and objects that 'The denial of capitalism's foundational status also reveals a culturalism in the postcolonialist argument': 'Without capitalism as the foundation for European power and the motive force of its globalization, Eurocentrism would have been just another ethnocentrism' (p. 346). Dirlik's main target is Gyan Prakash; Chakrabarty appears only in his notes (nn. 7, 12). The wider in-period debate, not aimed at him by name: Rosalind O'Hanlon and David Washbrook, 'After Orientalism: Culture, Criticism, and Politics in the Third World', Comparative Studies in Society and History 34:1 (1992), pp. 141–167. The body is closed access; only the publisher's first-page extract and the article's notes (as listed on Cambridge Core) were read. The extract calls Said's blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' in Indian colonial history, directions 'most recently and sharply endorsed in Gyan Prakash's discussion' (p. 141); a note objects that 'Prakash's notion of what constitutes Marxist history is problematic' (n. 13). None of the notes cites Chakrabarty. The 1.132 adversarial review, reading an OCR copy not consulted here, summarises their case as doubting that the post-foundational programme can sustain historical explanation and political agency, and as holding that Marxist and social historians had already historicised their categories. Prakash replied in the same issue (pp. 168–184). This is criticism of the wider programme, principally Prakash's; it is not evidence of a criticism of Chakrabarty. A contribution, not a founding: the book's epigraph takes 'provincialized' from Gadamer (p. 3), and the post entry already maps Said and Spivak; his argument 'follows directly from my involvement' in Subaltern Studies (p. 15). edge_096 (post → modern) and edge_124 (post → global) stay: they record the group's critiques, which already name him.

edge_916.relationship: Bengal jute-mill workers against universal class narratives: culture, hierarchy and the assumption of bourgeois equality in Marx's 'capital' (1989), taken up and contested by labour historians (1990–97)
edge_916.evidence_note: His own statement of the book's aim. Rethinking Working-Class History (1989), preface pp. xi–xv and introduction pp. 3–6, read in the publisher preview (imprint: copyright 1989; first paperback printing 2000; preface dated February 1988): 'In looking at this history in terms of Marx's categories, however, my objective is to develop a critical understanding of these categories themselves'; 'there is an assumption regarding “culture” built into Marx's category of “capital,” and much of what I have to say on Indian labor history, and labor history in general, follows from this reading of Marx' (p. xi); 'this book is an extended polemic against the reductionism' of political-economic analysis of culture, the 'common sense' of Marxist labour history in India; 'Culture, one might say, is the “unthought” of Indian Marxism' (p. xii). 'Perhaps we have long overestimated capitalism's need or capacity to homogenize the cultural conditions necessary for its own reproduction' (p. xiii). He keeps a commitment to equality: 'The struggle to be a “citizen” must be part of the struggle to be a “comrade”' (p. xiv). The figure of the worker in Marx 'was that of a person who belonged to a society where the bourgeois notion of equality was ingrained in culture' (p. 3), and 'there is no “working class” or “working-class consciousness” that ... “is either transcendental in relation to the field of events or runs in its empty sameness throughout the course of history”' (p. 6, quoting Foucault). He separates his argument from Thompson's: 'That my argument is not the same as Thompson's will be clear to any careful reader' (p. 5, n. 9). In-period reception by labour historians: Janaki Nair's review in International Labor and Working-Class History 37 (1990, pp. 96–99; not re-read here; the graph's verification note records that she recognises the theoretical contribution while questioning cultural determination, the treatment of traditions as survivals and the analysis of gender). Rajnarayan Chandavarkar, '“The Making of the Working Class”: E. P. Thompson and Indian History', History Workshop Journal 43 (1997; written for the 1994 History Workshop conference on Thompson; pp. 177–196 read): Thompson's 'inheritance' 'turned in Dipesh Chakrabarty's hands into a static, timeless, indeed Orientalist characterization of a “traditional” Indian, implicitly “Hindu” culture — in Bengal, a predominantly Muslim province' (p. 182); 'Bengali society, indeed Indian society, was now represented as England's proverbial Other' (p. 183); the view 'recently restated by Dipesh Chakrabarty, that rural migrants “imported a peasant culture into the industrial setting”' 'was not the product of an extensive investigation of the nature of labour migration' (pp. 184–185). Sarkar (1997, p. 87, page image checked) praises 'Dipesh Chakrabarty’s stimulating, if controversial, essays on Bengal labour history'; his n. 10 identifies them as the earlier Subaltern Studies essays 'Conditions for Knowledge of Working-Class Conditions: Employers, Government and the Jute-Workers of Calcutta, 1890–1940' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983) and 'Trade Unions in a Hierarchical Culture: The Jute Workers of Calcutta, 1920–50' (Subaltern Studies III, 1984), not the 1989 book. Nair (1990) and Chandavarkar (1997) are the in-period readings of the book itself. In 1992 he wrote that 'My book on working-class history struggles with the problem' of the transition narrative ('Artifice', p. 4). Context, not a genealogy: Eric Hobsbawm is among those he thanks for reading the manuscript (acknowledgments, p. xvii). edge_742 (subaltern → labourhistory) names him and Nair; see the proposed relabel. edge_358 (subaltern → social) stays.

edge_918.relationship: Climate change and the collapse of the distinction between natural and human history: humans as geological agents, species history and the history of capital (2009)
edge_918.evidence_note: Dated 2009, after the atlas's 1920–2000 frame: drafted after the user's decision of 2026-10-14 to end the 2000 break. No claim here concerns his work before 2000. 'The Climate of History: Four Theses', Critical Inquiry 35, no. 2 (Winter 2009), pp. 197–222, read in full. The first thesis: 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History' (p. 201). His readings in 'globalization, Marxist analysis of capital, subaltern studies, and postcolonial criticism ... had not really prepared me for making sense of this planetary conjuncture' (p. 199). On environmental history: 'the rise of environmental history in the late twentieth century made the breach wider', but 'environmental history, where it was not straightforwardly cultural, social, or economic history, looked upon human beings as biological agents', quoting Crosby's preface to The Columbian Exchange (p. 205); 'Scholars writing on the current climate-change crisis are indeed saying something significantly different from what environmental historians have said so far ... Humans now wield a geological force' (p. 206); the distinction between human and natural histories, 'much of which had been preserved even in environmental histories that saw the two entities in interaction—has begun to collapse' (p. 207). 'The mansion of modern freedoms stands on an ever-expanding base of fossil-fuel use' (p. 208). 'A critique that is only a critique of capital is not sufficient' (p. 212), yet 'the story of capital ... cannot be denied by recourse to the idea of species' (p. 219); the task is 'to mix together the immiscible chronologies of capital and species history' (p. 220). He ends with a 'negative universal history' (p. 222). Reception after 2009, labelled by date: Robert Emmett and Thomas Lekan, eds., Whose Anthropocene? Revisiting Dipesh Chakrabarty's 'Four Theses' (RCC Perspectives 2016/2, from a February 2015 workshop; read in part): the essay 'has become a primary text for understanding the problematic nature of the Anthropocene as a cultural category' (p. 7) and challenges 'ecological histories that situate humans as biological agents' (p. 8). The environmental historian Timothy J. LeCain (2016) writes, tentatively, that the theses 'may prove more radical than even he intended, or perhaps desires' (p. 15). Criticism: in his 2016 response Chakrabarty concedes to Carol Boggs that 'one can no longer separate the biological agency of humans from their geological agency in the way in which I appeared to do' (p. 104), and reports that 'Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg took me to task' over 'There are no lifeboats for the rich', quoting Kathleen McAfee: 'Contra Chakrabarty, the rich may face the same storms and they do have lifeboats' (p. 108). Malm and Hornborg (2014) are known here only through his response; their article is unread. A contribution that disputes the field's prior framing of human agency, not a founding claim for climate history.

edge_983.relationship: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’: the two senses of representation, the epistemic violence of colonial law and knowledge, and the subaltern woman silenced between colonial and indigenous patriarchal discourse on sati (1985–99)
edge_983.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988), read in the Williams and Chrisman reprint (pages of that reprint; its opening is abridged): ‘Some of the most radical criticism coming out of the West today is the result of an interested desire to conserve the subject of the West, or the West as Subject’ (p. 66). ‘Two senses of representation are being run together: representation as “speaking for”, as in politics, and representation as “re-presentation”, as in art or philosophy’; ‘representing them, the intellectuals represent themselves as transparent’ (p. 70); running vertreten and darstellen together ‘leads to an essentialist, utopian politics’ (p. 71). The codification of Hindu law is her ‘example of epistemic violence’ (pp. 76–77), and she asks whether, ‘inside and outside the circuit of the epistemic violence of imperialist law and education’, ‘can the subaltern speak?’ (p. 78). On sati she sets the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, which she says she ‘put together’ (p. 92), against ‘the Indian nativist argument’, ‘“The women actually wanted to die”’: ‘The two sentences go a long way to legitimize each other. One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness’ (p. 93). She qualifies: ‘Given that the abolition of sati was in itself admirable’ (p. 94); ‘Obviously I am not advocating the killing of widows’ (p. 97). ‘Between patriarchy and imperialism, subject-constitution and object-formation, the figure of the woman disappears ... into a violent shuttling’ (p. 102). She welcomes ‘all the information retrieval in these silenced areas’ in history and other disciplines, while warning that the assumed ‘consciousness or subject’ will ‘cohere with the work of imperialist subject-constitution’ (p. 90). The close: ‘The subaltern cannot speak. There is no virtue in global laundry lists with “woman” as a pious item. Representation has not withered away’ (reprint p. 104, OCR damaged, wording restored from the unpaginated 1988 text in Morris, 2010; 1988 p. 308 per Sunder Rajan in the same volume). She credits Lata Mani’s 1983 thesis on sati as ‘a brilliant account’ and ‘profited from discussion with Ms Mani’ (n. 65, p. 109). The 1999 revision (A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, ch. 3; read in Morris’s unpaginated reprint; CPR p. 308 per Sunder Rajan) says: ‘in the first version of this text, I wrote, in the accents of passionate lament: the subaltern cannot speak! It was an inadvisable remark’, and that Bhubaneswari Bhaduri ‘was not a “true” subaltern’. ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (Critical Inquiry, 1985, read pp. 243–245) opens: ‘It should not be possible to read nineteenth-century British literature without remembering that imperialism, understood as England’s social mission, was a crucial part of the cultural representation of England to the English’, and finds it ‘particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism’ (p. 243). In-period readings by historians: Gyan Prakash, ‘Can the “Subaltern” Ride?’ (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint 2000, pp. 226–227, read): ‘as Spivak states starkly, the debate left no room for the woman’s enunciatory position’; ‘Spivak very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman as the point at which the interpreter must acknowledge the limits of historical understanding’. Sumit Sarkar, ‘Orientalism Revisited’ (Oxford Literary Review, 1994; reprint p. 254, n. 14, read), criticising Mani’s Saidian assumptions, contrasts ‘the much more substantive discussion of pre-colonial and colonial discourses on sati in Spivak’. Contested in period: Terry Eagleton (LRB, 13 May 1999; web text, no page numbers, read) on A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ to be the critique its title promises, ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’, yet ‘this study boldly addresses the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’; he reports that she contrasts her own critique with Aijaz Ahmad’s ‘scorching assault’ in In Theory (1992; unread here). Benita Parry, ‘Problems in Current Theories of Colonial Discourse’, Oxford Literary Review 9 (1987), pp. 27–58, is the best-known in-period critique; it is closed access and unread, and no claim is made about its argument. A contribution, not a founding: the post entry already lists Said (1978) before her, and edge_107 (language → post) and edge_115 (subaltern → post) stay.

edge_984.relationship: A critique from within: the collective's recovery of subaltern consciousness read as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', Guha's 'full autonomy' questioned, and woman shown to be 'the neglected syntagm' of its accounts of insurgency (1985–88)
edge_984.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’, Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363, read in full: the group ‘offers a theory of change’, plotting change ‘as confrontations rather than transition’ (p. 330); its practice is ‘closer to deconstruction’ than its self-description (p. 332); ‘This is why I hope to align them with deconstruction’ (p. 336). ‘Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain’ (p. 341), she reads the project to retrieve subaltern consciousness ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’ (p. 342), which ‘would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness’ (p. 356). On gender: ‘The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women’, but ‘I think they overlook how important the concept-metaphor woman is to the functioning of their discourse’ (p. 356); ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357); ‘Male subaltern and historian are here united in the common assumption that the procreative sex is a species apart’ (p. 358); ‘woman is the neglected syntagm of the semiosis of subalternity of insurgency’ (p. 359); ‘if the question of female subaltern consciousness ... is a red herring, the question of subaltern consciousness as such must be judged a red herring as well’ (p. 360). She qualifies: ‘The making-visible of the figure of woman is perhaps not a task that the group should fairly be asked to perform’, but ‘a feminist historian of the subaltern must raise the question of woman as a structural rather than marginal issue’ (p. 361). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha’s ‘autonomous domain’, ‘I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy’ (p. 79); ‘the colonized subaltern subject is irretrievably heterogeneous’ (p. 79); ‘If, in the context of colonial production, the subaltern has no history and cannot speak, the subaltern as female is even more deeply in shadow’ (pp. 82–83). In-period readings from historians of the field: Rosalind O’Hanlon, ‘Recovering the Subject’ (Modern Asian Studies, 1988; Verso reprint, read), takes up her phrase (p. 80, citing SS IV p. 342) but warns ‘we should certainly hesitate before accepting Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s suggestion that the strategy of the Subaltern series “in claiming a positive subject-position for the subaltern might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times”’ (p. 105, citing SS IV p. 345). Gyanendra Pandey, a member, reads the 1988 close as Gramsci’s point: ‘“The subaltern cannot speak,” writes Gayatri Spivak, making, I suggest, much the same point’ (Ethnos, 1995; reprint p. 285, read). Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that the 1988 essay ‘brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies’ and ‘may have provided a major impetus’ for the gender and voice themes of Subaltern Studies IX (1996). Her own later account (‘The New Subaltern’, 2000, read): ‘Except in the work of Susie Tharu ... Subaltern Studies is not informed by feminist theory as such’ (p. 325), and of 1985, ‘Subaltern Studies had no need of such apologetics. But the theoretically inclined metropolitan identitarians did’ (p. 332). Later reading, labelled: Partha Chatterjee (2010; Morris volume, unpaginated) recalls first reading both essays in 1985 with ‘bewilderment’ and calls her intervention ‘the poststructuralist moment in Subaltern Studies’, adding that a changed political context also drove the shift. A critique from within, not a rejection: she joined the editorial collective in the 1990s. edge_389 (gender → subaltern) carries the same story under the gender entry; see the proposed relabel. Guha’s person edge (pe137_guha_rel_01, guha draft) cites the same 1985 essay as reception; this edge is hers.

durkheim.label: Social facts & collective life
durkheim.date_label: Division of Labour 1893 · Rules 1895 · Elementary Forms 1912 · later school
durkheim.description: Social facts, causes and functions, solidarity, ritual and collective thought provide distinct sociological questions. Hubert, Mauss, Simiand, Halbwachs and Meillet develop particular inquiries; historical and anthropological recipients adapt them selectively.
durkheim.representative_figures_and_works: Émile Durkheim (1858–1917), The Division of Labour in Society (1893); influence on Bloch is substantial but selective and critical.

representative_people.context: Defines a sociological object, distinguishes causes from functions, and investigates conditions of solidarity and collective thought. His arguments and ethnographic assumptions require separate assessment.
representative_people.works: De la division du travail social (1893); Les Règles de la méthode sociologique (1895); Les Formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse (1912)

representative_people.context: Collaborative research on sacrifice and later work on gifts examine ritual relations and obligations; the two projects are not interchangeable.
representative_people.works: With Henri Hubert, “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899); “Essai sur le don” (1925)

representative_people.context: Coauthors a provisional comparative theory of sacrifice that distinguishes participants, consecration and mediation. His contribution is not absorbed into Mauss’s later gift essay.
representative_people.works: With Marcel Mauss, “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899)

representative_people.context: Pursues the methodological relation between historical evidence and social science. Annales explicitly reprints his intervention in 1960 as part of its continuing dialogue.
representative_people.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903; Annales reprint, 1960)

representative_people.context: Develops the social frameworks of remembering as a distinct inquiry. Later critical reuse and his intellectual formation are separate evidentiary questions.
representative_people.works: Les Cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); On Collective Memory (edited English collection, 1992)

representative_people.context: Explicitly applies Durkheim’s social-fact definition to language and investigates social conditions of semantic change.
representative_people.works: “Comment les mots changent de sens” (1906)

representative_people.context: A selective historical recipient and interlocutor, not a doctrinal adherent. His acknowledgment of Durkheim is documented in the scholarly introduction cited here.
representative_people.works: Feudal Society (1939–40); contextual reception study: Susan W. Friedman, Marc Bloch, Sociology and Geography

durkheim.scope_note: Durkheim and selected collaborators, recipients and interlocutors, not a membership register. Collective explanation does not imply that all institutions are useful or all differentiation creates solidarity. Colonial-era categories and ethnographic generalizations remain claims to assess. Bloch’s engagement is selective; modernization and Bourdieu links still need more precise reception passages.

strands.title: Social facts and institutional resistance
strands.focus: Durkheim’s examples include obligations, signs and monetary practices. Externality and coercive capacity distinguish his object; mere statistical commonness does not suffice.

strands.title: Origins, functions and critical antecedents
strands.focus: Chapter V disputes Comte’s and Spencer’s utility-based explanations: identifying a use does not explain an institution’s origin, and functions can change.

strands.title: Differentiation and failures of solidarity
strands.focus: Division of labor can produce conflict and anomie. Durkheim’s discussion of crises and capital/labor antagonism qualifies any automatic equation of differentiation with cohesion.
strands.works: Division of Labour (1893), book III chapter I

strands.title: Religious life and collective categories
strands.focus: Sacred practices and collective membership are distinguished from a purely private belief. The proposed social formation of categories is an argument to assess, not an established origin of all thought.
strands.works: Elementary Forms (1912), introduction and religion definition

strands.title: Sacrifice, participants and mediation
strands.focus: Hubert and Mauss build on and revise earlier comparative scholarship. Their provisional model distinguishes ritual participants and movement between sacred and profane.
strands.works: “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899)

strands.title: Historical evidence and social science
strands.focus: Simiand’s methodological challenge and Bloch’s selective historical reception are different forms of engagement; Annales’ later reprint makes one continuing exchange explicit.
strands.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903; reprinted 1960); Bloch reception in Sociology and Geography

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering and language
strands.focus: Halbwachs’s memory inquiry and Meillet’s semantic history develop different objects from social relations. Shared vocabulary alone does not establish identical methods.
strands.works: Les Cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); “Comment les mots changent de sens” (1906)

anthropology.description: Ethnographic observation, comparison, historical reconstruction and interpretation generate different accounts of social life. environment.label: Environmental history
environment.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model. Bullard’s environmental-justice inquiry and Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life histories broaden comparison toward unequal burdens, displacement and authority over historical accounts. Dust Bowl debates distinguish agricultural capitalism, technology and soils, federal intervention, regional scale and household survival; primary criticism and later social history complicate a single causal summary.
environment.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

environment.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community.

latour.label: Bruno Latour / laboratory studies
latour.description: Studies the practical work through which scientific claims become established facts, including experiments, inscriptions, instruments, and relations among researchers. Laboratory ethnography offers a route into science studies that should not be collapsed into textual interpretation or into Bloor’s programme. The Pasteur study extends his inquiry into historical scientific change and distinguishes that analysis from an explanation by social forces alone. historicism.label: Historicism & idealist philosophies of history
historicism.description: Groups related arguments for historical specificity and interpretive understanding. German Historismus and British and Italian idealism are not one doctrine: Collingwood’s re-enactment is a particular account of historical thought, not a method shared by everyone here. This usage differs from Popper’s criticism of predictive laws of historical development. Approaches separate documentary interpretation, the human sciences, living historical questions, developmental individuality and rethinking past arguments; their disagreements concern evidence, values, political power and historical context.

dipesh_chakrabarty.label: Dipesh Chakrabarty
dipesh_chakrabarty.date_label: Rethinking Working-Class History 1989 · “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History” 1992 · Provincializing Europe 2000 · “The Climate of History” 2009
dipesh_chakrabarty.description: A historian of modern South Asia in the Subaltern Studies collective. He argues that, within university-based historical discourse, an imagined 'Europe' remains its dominant theoretical reference: 'the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call “Indian,” “Chinese,” “Kenyan”', where 'Europe' and 'India' are 'hyperreal terms', figures of the imaginary 'subject to contestation' (1992). Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) reads Bengal’s jute-mill workers against an assumption of 'a hegemonic bourgeois culture' in Marx’s category of capital. 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (1992) calls Europe 'a silent referent in historical knowledge', and Provincializing Europe (2000) criticises the historicist 'first in Europe, then elsewhere' that placed colonized peoples in 'an imaginary waiting room of history', while holding European thought 'both indispensable and inadequate'; a 2000 essay separates History 1, the past 'posited by capital', from History 2, pasts that are 'not pasts separate from capital' but 'inhere in capital and yet interrupt and punctuate' its logic. In period, Sumit Sarkar called the trajectory he described 'debilitating', and the labour historian Rajnarayan Chandavarkar found a 'static, timeless, indeed Orientalist' culture in his Bengal book. After 2000, 'The Climate of History' (2009) argued that climate change spells 'the collapse of the age-old humanist distinction between natural history and human history'.
dipesh_chakrabarty.representative_figures_and_works: Dipesh Chakrabarty (b. 1948); Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (1989); “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History: Who Speaks for ‘Indian’ Pasts?” (Representations, 1992); “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (Perspectives, 1997); Provincializing Europe: Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference (2000); “Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital” (Public Culture, 2000). After 2000: “The Climate of History: Four Theses” (Critical Inquiry, 2009). Readings: Nair’s review (1990); Dirlik (1994); Chandavarkar (1997); Sarkar (1997); Whose Anthropocene? (2016), with his response.
dipesh_chakrabarty.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the 1989 preface (pp. xi–xv) and introduction (pp. 3–6) in the publisher preview; 'Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History' (Representations 37, 1992, pp. 1–26) in full; the 1997 AHA essay in full (web text, no page numbers); the Provincializing Europe introduction (pp. 3–23, in the publisher’s excerpt); 'Universalism and Belonging in the Logic of Capital' (Public Culture, 2000), which he describes as a slightly different version of the book’s chapter 2; and 'The Climate of History' (2009) in full. The rest of the 1989 and 2000 books is unread, including chapter 2 itself. He is not presented as a founder. He calls Ranajit Guha 'the founder of the group' (1997) and writes that his 'argument for provincializing Europe follows directly from my involvement in this project' (2000, p. 15). The book’s critique of historicism builds on Guha’s rejection of Hobsbawm’s 'prepolitical' and cites Fabian’s 'denial of coevalness' (pp. 8, 11–15). O'Hanlon and Washbrook (1992) criticised the wider post-Orientalist programme, principally Prakash's, without naming him; only their opening page and notes were read. The 2009 essay and its reception (2014–16) are after 2000 and support only the separate environment edge, which is dated 2009 in its label and text; they are not evidence for any claim about his work before 2000.

ranajit_guha.label: Ranajit Guha
ranajit_guha.date_label: A Rule of Property for Bengal 1963 · “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” 1982 · Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency 1983 · “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency” 1983 · “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography” 1989 (book 1997)
ranajit_guha.description: A historian of colonial India, who taught at Sussex and the Australian National University and edited Subaltern Studies from its first volume (1982) until he left the editorial team in 1988. The opening statement holds that the historiography of Indian nationalism 'has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism', and that it leaves out 'the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain' that 'neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', while allowing 'a great deal of overlap' between the two (1982). Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983) attributes 'a consciousness' to the rebel peasant, holds that Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India', and reads that consciousness through the records of counter-insurgency; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (1983) finds colonial, nationalist and radical histories alike making the rebel 'only a contingent element in another history with another subject'. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989; book 1997) defines hegemony, against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony', as dominance in which 'Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)', and argues that colonial dominance had 'quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony'. In period, Spivak (1985) read the recovery of subaltern consciousness as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', O'Hanlon (1988) found 'the classic figure of Western humanism' readmitted 'in the figure of the subaltern himself', Bayly (1988) found that the approach sometimes seemed to postulate an 'unchanging peasantry', and Sarkar (1997) an 'unnoticed drift' towards nationalist positions 'even in Guha's initial formulation of the project'.
ranajit_guha.representative_figures_and_works: Ranajit Guha (1923–2023); A Rule of Property for Bengal: An Essay on the Idea of Permanent Settlement (Paris: Mouton, 1963); Preface and “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India”, Subaltern Studies I (1982); Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (Delhi, 1983); “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency”, Subaltern Studies II (1983); “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography”, Subaltern Studies VI (1989), and Dominance without Hegemony: History and Power in Colonial India (1997); Selected Subaltern Studies, edited with Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (1988). Readings: Spivak (1985); O'Hanlon (1988); Bayly (1988); Sarkar (1997); Chakrabarty (2000).
ranajit_guha.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the Subaltern Studies I preface and opening statement in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (1988, pp. 35–44); the introduction of Elementary Aspects (pp. 1–17), its bibliography and pp. 89–90; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983, pp. 1–42) in full; and 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (Subaltern Studies VI, 1989), pp. 210–215, 227–233, 276–277, 291–292 and 299–303. The 1963 and 1997 books are known here only from metadata and from later quotation; the rest of Elementary Aspects and of the 1989 essay is unread. He is not presented as the founder of a field. In period, Chakrabarty called him 'the founder of the group' (1997) and James C. Scott wrote that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document' of 'the Subaltern Studies School', while finding 'school' too rigid a term (1999); his own 1982 statement claims 'no more than to try and indicate an orientation'. Contested in period by Spivak (1985, a reading from within the project), O'Hanlon (1988), Bayly (1988) and Sarkar (1997); Javeed Alam's Marxist critique (Social Scientist, 1983) is known only through O'Hanlon and is unread. Vinay Bahl (1997) is unread. Chakrabarty's 2000 account of the project is a member's later reading and carries no edge alone. Not Ramachandra Guha, the environmental historian, who has a separate people record.

gayatri_chakravorty_spivak.label: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
gayatri_chakravorty_spivak.date_label: Of Grammatology (translation) 1976 · “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography” 1985 · “Three Women’s Texts” 1985 · “Can the Subaltern Speak?” 1988 · A Critique of Postcolonial Reason 1999
gayatri_chakravorty_spivak.description: A literary theorist and the translator of Derrida’s Of Grammatology (1976), whose essays on colonial India became reference points for historians. In ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ (1985) she read the collective ‘from within but against the grain’, proposing that its recovery of subaltern consciousness be read ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’, and argued that it overlooked ‘how important the concept-metaphor woman is’ to its own discourse. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988) separates representation as ‘speaking for’ from ‘re-presentation’, argues that in Foucault and Deleuze’s conversation intellectuals, ‘representing them, ... represent themselves as transparent’, and reads the British abolition of sati through the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, set against the nativist ‘The women actually wanted to die’: between them ‘One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness.’ She later called the essay’s closing ‘the subaltern cannot speak!’ ‘an inadvisable remark’ (1999). In period, Gyan Prakash (1992) held that she ‘very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman’ as a limit of historical understanding, Rosalind O’Hanlon (1988) urged hesitation ‘before accepting’ her proposal to re-inscribe the series’ strategy ‘as a strategy for our times’, and Terry Eagleton (1999), crediting the book with addressing ‘the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’, found her Critique ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ and ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’.
gayatri_chakravorty_spivak.representative_figures_and_works: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (b. 1942); translator’s preface to Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1976); “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography” (Subaltern Studies IV, 1985; introduction to Selected Subaltern Studies, 1988); “Three Women’s Texts and a Critique of Imperialism” (Critical Inquiry, 1985); “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (in Nelson and Grossberg, eds., Marxism and the Interpretation of Culture, 1988; revised in A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, 1999); “The New Subaltern: A Silent Interview” (2000). Readings: O’Hanlon (1988); Chakrabarty (1992); Prakash (1992); Sarkar (1994); Pandey (1995); Eagleton (1999); Chatterjee (2010).
gayatri_chakravorty_spivak.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ in the 1988 text as reprinted in Williams and Chrisman, Colonial Discourse and Post-Colonial Theory (1993; pp. 66–111, opening abridged), with page numbers of that reprint; two 1988 page anchors (p. 277 and p. 308) come from Chakrabarty (1992, n. 48) and Sunder Rajan (2010). The 1999 revision was read in Morris’s 2010 reprint, which has no page numbers. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ was read in Subaltern Studies IV (1985), pp. 330–363, in full; ‘Three Women’s Texts’ pp. 243–245; the translator’s preface to Of Grammatology at p. lxxvii of the 1997 corrected edition. She is a literary critic, not a historian, and is not presented as a founder of postcolonial studies; she joined the Subaltern Studies editorial collective in the 1990s (Chaturvedi gives Subaltern Studies IX, 1996; Chatterjee recalls 1993) and in 2000 called herself ‘a sometime member’. Benita Parry’s in-period critique (Oxford Literary Review, 1987), Aijaz Ahmad’s In Theory (1992) and Lata Mani’s work on sati (1987, 1998) were not read; Ahmad appears only through Eagleton’s report of her contrast with him. Chatterjee (2010) is a later reading by a member of the collective and carries no in-period claim.
